case_info.scenario: An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

       history would make it stronger."

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
